targets.name: Barnard's Star
targets.note: The fastest-moving star on the sky: 10.3 arcsec per year, about 1.7 SPHEREx pixels per year. Six light years away. The classic proper-motion target.
targets.look_for: Watch the bright star at the centre creep upwards (north) against the fixed background: 10.4 arcsec a year, about 1.7 SPHEREx pixels — the fastest motion of any star in the sky.
targets.epoch_note: Centred on Gaia DR3's position carried forward to 2025-09-07. Its J2000 position is 4.4 arcmin south, outside this view.

targets.name: Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb
targets.note: A pair of brown dwarfs (T1 + T6) orbiting the nearby star Epsilon Indi A, about 400 arcsec away from it. Cold, methane-rich, and bright in the near infrared.
targets.look_for: Two failed stars too small to burn, orbiting each other — the dot at the centre, drifting down and to the left (south-east) at 4.7 arcsec a year. They give off most of their light in the infrared: click the dot for its spectrum.
targets.epoch_note: Centred on Gaia DR3's position for Epsilon Indi Ba carried forward to 2025-09-07, about 2 arcmin from its 2MASS-era (1999) position.

targets.name: WISE 0855-0714
targets.note: The coldest known brown dwarf, 250 K, 7.5 light years away. Moves about 8 arcsec per year. Water-ice clouds. Position as given in the challenge brief.
targets.look_for: The coldest brown dwarf known, about -23 C. The brief's position is from 2010; by 2025 it has moved 2 arcmin west (right of centre), to within 8 arcsec of a brighter star that SPHEREx's 6-arcsec pixels cannot cleanly separate from it.
targets.epoch_note: The position given in the challenge brief, used verbatim. It is from 2010-era WISE data and WISE 0855 is too cold for Gaia, so it is not carried forward.

targets.name: RW Aurigae
targets.note: A young binary T Tauri star that dims by magnitudes for months at a time when its tidally disrupted disc passes in front of it. Brightness, not position, is the story.
targets.look_for: This one does not move — it blinks. A newborn star whose dusty disc has been torn by a passing companion; when a streamer of that dust drifts across our line of sight the star fades for months. Watch its brightness, not its position.
targets.kind: young star with a torn disc

targets.name: R Draconis
targets.note: A Mira variable: a pulsating red giant that swings about 8 magnitudes over a 245-day period. Enormous in the near infrared.
targets.look_for: A dying red giant that swells and shrinks over about 245 days, changing brightness by a factor of a thousand. It is so bright here that its core saturates the detector — click slightly off-centre for a spectrum.

targets.name: Proxima Centauri
targets.note: The nearest star. 3.85 arcsec per year of proper motion plus a large parallax wobble.
targets.look_for: The closest star to the Sun, with a known planet in its habitable zone. It both drifts and wobbles, because it is near enough that Earth's own orbit shifts its apparent position.

targets.name: Luhman 16 AB
targets.note: The nearest brown dwarf binary, 6.5 light years away, moving 2.8 arcsec per year.
targets.look_for: The nearest pair of brown dwarfs, 6.5 light years away, with weather: one of them has clouds that change its brightness as it rotates.

targets.name: Teegarden's Star
targets.note: A nearby red dwarf with two temperate planets and 5 arcsec per year of proper motion.
targets.look_for: A small, cool red dwarf 12 light years away with two planets that could hold liquid water. It moves noticeably against the background.
targets.epoch_note: Centred on Gaia DR3's position carried forward to 2025-09-07.
